o: The classic way to find the girth of an undirected graph: run a BFS from every vertex. During a BFS rooted at s, whenever we scan an edge (u,v) where v is already visited and v is not u's BFS-tree parent, we've found a cycle through s of length dist[u] + dist[v] + 1. Taking the minimum over all roots and edges gives the shortest cycle. With n, m <= 1000, O(n*(n+m)) is about 2e6 operations — comfortably fast. Both examples confirm: two triangles give 3, a forest gives -1.
k: Girth via BFS from every source: a non-tree edge encountered during BFS closes a cycle of length dist[u]+dist[v]+1.
Skip the tree-parent edge to avoid counting the 2-edge back-and-forth as a cycle.
O(n·(n+m)) is fine for n, m <= 1000.

a.i: For each root, BFS records distances and parents; any cross edge to an already-visited non-parent vertex yields a candidate cycle length.
s: For each source s, run BFS storing dist and parent.
On edge (u,v) with v visited and parent[u] != v, update best = min(best, dist[u]+dist[v]+1).
a.t: O(n·(n+m)) — a full BFS per vertex
a.sp: O(n+m) for adjacency, dist, and parent arrays

w: The parent check is essential; without it every edge looks like a length-2 cycle. The formula can overestimate slightly for some root choices but never underestimates, and the true girth is always witnessed by some root, so the minimum is correct. Follow-up: weighted graphs need Dijkstra-based girth (O(n·m log n)).
